On June 6, 2023, Twitch announced restrictions on third-party sponsor placements in streams, including restricting the size of sponsor logos, and prohibiting "burned-in" audio, video, or [[Display advertising|display]] advertising. The changes were met with criticism from major streamers such as [[Asmongold]] (who threatened to leave the service), [[MoistCr1tikal]], and [[VShojo|Zentreya]] due to their broad wording, concerns that it would impact streamers' existing relationships with advertisers, and their impact on charity and esports events that rely extensively on sponsorship. The service quickly retracted the new branded content policy and announced that it would be clarified, stating that it was intended to "clarify our existing ads policy that was intended to prohibit third party ad networks from selling burned in video and display ads on Twitch, which is consistent with other services", and that Twitch "[does] not intend to limit streamers' ability to enter into direct relationships with sponsors."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Alexander |first=Cristina |date=2023-06-06 |title=Twitch Crackdown on Creator Ads Sparks Calls for Boycotts and Protests |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/twitch-crackdown-on-creator-ads-sparks-calls-for-boycotts-and-protests |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=IGN |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Wood |first1=Austin |last2=Bailey |first2=Dustin |date=2023-06-06 |title=Twitch streamers up in arms as new advertising rules limit sponsors and threaten to kill charity and esports events |url=https://www.gamesradar.com/twitch-streamers-up-in-arms-as-new-advertising-rules-limit-sponsors-and-threaten-to-kill-charity-and-esports-events/ |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=gamesradar |language=en}}</ref>

In August 2023, Twitch began to trial a "Discovery Feed" feature in its mobile apps, populated by "featured" clips from followed users.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Peters |first=Jay |date=2023-08-22 |title=Twitch is testing a TikTok-style feed |url=https://www.theverge.com/2023/8/22/23842075/twitch-tiktok-style-discovery-feed |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=The Verge |language=en}}</ref> In October 2023, Twitch began to implement [[Story (social media)|stories]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parrish |first=Ash |date=2023-10-16 |title=Twitch adds stories to its mobile app |url=https://www.theverge.com/2023/10/16/23919304/twitch-stories-roll-out-twitchcon-2023 |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=The Verge |language=en}}</ref> At TwitchCon 2023, Twitch announced upcoming updates to its Guest Star feature (concurrently renamed "Stream Together") to allow for merged chat rooms, and that streamers under an affiliation or partnership agreement with the service (unless contractually required) would be allowed to simulcast their streams on competing platforms such as YouTube, as opposed to only mobile-centric video platforms.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Peters |first=Jay |date=2023-10-20 |title=Twitch will now let streamers simultaneously stream on any service they want |url=https://www.theverge.com/2023/10/20/23926013/twitch-simultaneously-stream-any-service-platform-twitchcon |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=The Verge |language=en}}</ref>

On December 6, 2023, Twitch announced that it would exit the South Korea market effective February 27, 2024, citing the prohibitive costs of offering the service in the country.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hyeong-woo |first=Kan |date=2022-04-21 |title=[Newsmaker] YouTube threatens to cut down investments in Korea over 'network usage fee' bill |url=https://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20220421000740 |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=The Korea Herald |language=en}}</ref> Due to demands from internet service providers that Twitch pay network access fees, Twitch restricted streams to [[720p]] quality in September 2022, and blocked access to video-on-demand (VOD) content (including archived broadcasts and clips) in February 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Murray |first=Sean |date=2022-09-29 |title=Twitch Responds To Korean Government Bill By Limiting Stream Quality To 720p |url=https://www.thegamer.com/twitch-korea-limiting-stream-quality-to-720p/ |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=TheGamer |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-01-30 |title=Twitch to be switched off in Korea for VOD from Feb. 7 |url=https://koreajoongangdaily.joins.com/2023/01/30/business/industry/Twitch/20230130190544807.html |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=Korea JoongAng Daily |language=en}}</ref> Users in South Korea will no longer be allowed to monetize their streams, and will be offboarded from the affiliate and partnership programs.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dong-woo |first=Chang |date=2023-12-06 |title=Twitch plans to shut down in S. Korea over high network costs |url=https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20231206002600320 |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=Yonhap News Agency |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Impact of Twitch Shutdown in Korea on Users Outside of Korea |url=https://help.twitch.tv/s/article/korea-update-nonkr?language=en_US&%24web_only=true&_branch_match_id=1260749383115248951&_branch_referrer=H4sIAAAAAAAAA8soKSkottLXLynPLEnO0C1PTdJLLCjQy8nMy9ZP1ffzcc93KqtyinRNAgBauUQ%2FKQAAAA%3D%3D |access-date=2023-12-06 |website=help.twitch.tv}}</ref> In February 2024, Twitch was additionally fined [[South Korean won|₩]]435 million ($327,067) by the Korea Telecommunications Commission, deeming Twitch's degradation of service in the country to be unjustified and undermining the interests of users.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-02-23 |title=Korea slaps $327,067 fine on Twitch for suspending service |url=https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/www/tech/2024/02/419_369371.html |access-date=2024-02-25 |website=[[The Korea Times]] |language=en}}</ref>

In January 2024, Twitch announced another [[2023–2024 video game industry layoffs|mass layoff]], affecting 500 employees or 35% of total staff, after previous layoffs in early 2023.<ref>{{Cite news |last=D'Anastasio |first=Cecilia |title=Amazon's Twitch to Cut 500 Employees, About 35% of Staff |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-01-09/amazon-s-twitch-to-cut-500-employees-about-35-of-staff |access-date=2024-01-10 |newspaper=Bloomberg |date=January 9, 2024 |archive-date=January 9, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240109224451/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-01-09/amazon-s-twitch-to-cut-500-employees-about-35-of-staff |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=A Difficult Update about our Workforce |url=https://blog.twitch.tv/en/2024/01/10/a-difficult-update-about-our-workforce/ |access-date=2024-01-11 |website=blog.twitch.tv |language=en |archive-date=June 11, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240611090520/https://blog.twitch.tv/en/2024/01/10/a-difficult-update-about-our-workforce/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The announcement came amid ongoing struggles and ensuing layoffs across the [[Tech industry|tech]] and [[Digital media companies|digital media]] sectors.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Duffy |first=Clare |date=2024-01-10 |title=Game streaming firm Twitch cutting 500 jobs {{!}} CNN Business |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/01/10/tech/twitch-cutting-500-jobs/index.html |access-date=2024-01-10 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref>

In October 2024, Twitch's longtime head of music Cindy Charles died.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://variety.com/2024/digital/news/cindy-charles-twitch-head-of-music-dead-1236182855/|first=Jem|last=Aswad|title=Cindy Charles, Twitch's Head of Music and Longtime Digital Music Executive, Dies at 69 |publisher=Variety|date=October 18, 2024|access-date=October 18, 2024}}</ref>

== Content ==
Twitch is designed to be a platform for content, including [[esports]] tournaments, personal streams of individual players, and gaming-related talk shows.<ref>{{cite web|last=Miller|first=Patrick|date=October 31, 2011|title=Twitch.tv Releases iPhone App, Feeds Your Addiction|url=http://www.pcworld.com/article/242753/twitchtv_releases_iphone_app_feeds_your_addiction.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120820025152/http://www.pcworld.com/article/242753/twitchtv_releases_iphone_app_feeds_your_addiction.html|archive-date=August 20, 2012|access-date=July 25, 2014|work=PC World}}</ref> A number of channels do live [[speedrunning]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Sebastian Haley|date=February 5, 2013|title=Can live speedruns compete with e-sports? (interview)|url=https://venturebeat.com/2013/02/05/twitch-tv-speedrun-interview/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201231628/http://venturebeat.com/2013/02/05/twitch-tv-speedrun-interview/|archive-date=February 1, 2014|access-date=January 23, 2014|website=VentureBeat}}</ref> The Twitch homepage currently displays games based on viewership.<ref name="Webb-2012"/> {{As of|2018|6|post=,}} some of the most popular games streamed on Twitch are ''[[Fortnite]]'', ''[[Grand Theft Auto V]]'', ''[[League of Legends]]'', ''[[Dota 2]]'', ''[[PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds]]'', ''[[Hearthstone]]'', ''[[Overwatch (2016 video game)|Overwatch]]'' and ''[[Counter-Strike: Global Offensive]]'' with a combined total of over 356 million hours watched.{{citation needed|date=June 2024}}

Twitch has also made expansions into non-gaming content; such as in July 2013, the site streamed a performance of 'Fester's Feast' from [[San Diego Comic-Con]], and on July 30, 2014, [[electronic dance music]] act [[Steve Aoki]] broadcast a live performance from a nightclub in [[Ibiza]].<ref>{{cite web|date=July 15, 2013|title=Twitch to stream Video Games Live concert from Comic-Con|url=http://www.polygon.com/2013/7/15/4525762/twitch-to-stream-video-games-live-concert-from-comic-con|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141011050737/http://www.polygon.com/2013/7/15/4525762/twitch-to-stream-video-games-live-concert-from-comic-con|archive-date=October 11, 2014|access-date=August 8, 2014|website=Polygon}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Twitch tries out live concerts with free house music performance tonight|work=The Verge|url=https://www.theverge.com/2014/7/30/5953217/twitch-tries-music-with-free-steve-aoki-concert-tonight|url-status=live|access-date=August 8, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140802035436/http://www.theverge.com/2014/7/30/5953217/twitch-tries-music-with-free-steve-aoki-concert-tonight|archive-date=August 2, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=DJ Steve Aoki to star in Twitch's first live concert tonight|url=http://www.cnet.com/news/steve-aoki-to-star-in-twitchs-first-live-concert-tonight/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140802150307/http://www.cnet.com/news/steve-aoki-to-star-in-twitchs-first-live-concert-tonight/|archive-date=August 2, 2014|access-date=August 8, 2014|website=CNET}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Twitch starts streaming live music today|work=Polygon|url=http://www.polygon.com/2014/7/30/5952191/twitch-starts-streaming-live-music-today|url-status=live|access-date=August 8, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140803071652/http://www.polygon.com/2014/7/30/5952191/twitch-starts-streaming-live-music-today|archive-date=August 3, 2014}}</ref> In January 2015, Twitch introduced an official category for music streams, such as radio shows and music production activities, and in March 2015, announced that it would become the new official live-streaming partner of the [[Ultra Music Festival]], an [[electronic music festival]] in [[Miami]].<ref name="PC World-2015"/><ref>{{cite web|date=March 23, 2015|title=The Ultra Music Festival will be broadcast live on Twitch|url=https://www.theverge.com/2015/3/23/8277547/the-ultra-music-festival-will-be-broadcast-live-on-twitch|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150325141952/http://www.theverge.com/2015/3/23/8277547/the-ultra-music-festival-will-be-broadcast-live-on-twitch|archive-date=March 25, 2015|access-date=March 25, 2015|website=The Verge}}</ref>

On October 28, 2015, Twitch launched a second non-gaming category, "Creative", which is intended for streams showcasing the creation of artistic and creative works. To promote the launch, the service also streamed an eight-day [[Marathon (television)|marathon]] of [[Bob Ross]]{{'}} ''[[The Joy of Painting]]''.<ref>{{cite web|date=October 29, 2015|title=Twitch launches "Creative" category, eight-day Bob Ross Painting marathon|url=https://arstechnica.com/business/2015/10/twitch-launches-creative-category-eight-day-bob-ross-painting-marathon/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151030025453/http://arstechnica.com/business/2015/10/twitch-launches-creative-category-eight-day-bob-ross-painting-marathon/|archive-date=October 30, 2015|access-date=December 28, 2015|website=Ars Technica}}</ref> In July 2016, Twitch launched "Social eating" as a beta; it was inspired by the Korean phenomenon of [[mukbang]] and Korean players having engaged in the practice as intermissions on their gaming streams.<ref>{{cite web|date=July 11, 2016|title=Why eating and gaming is a thing on Twitch|url=http://www.polygon.com/2016/7/11/12149446/twitch-social-eating-interview|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160714091550/http://www.polygon.com/2016/7/11/12149446/twitch-social-eating-interview|archive-date=July 14, 2016|access-date=July 18, 2016|website=Polygon|publisher=Vox Media}}</ref>

{{Anchor|IRL}}In March 2017, Twitch added an "IRL" category, which is designed for content within Twitch guidelines that does not fall within any of the other established categories on the site (such as [[lifelog]]s).<ref>{{cite web|date=March 12, 2017|title=Games Are Taking A Back Seat To Players On Video Game Streaming Sites|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/alltechconsidered/2017/03/12/514107238/are-taking-a-backseat-to-players-on-video-game-streaming-sites|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170812022259/http://www.npr.org/sections/alltechconsidered/2017/03/12/514107238/are-taking-a-backseat-to-players-on-video-game-streaming-sites|archive-date=August 12, 2017|access-date=August 11, 2017|website=[[NPR]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Byers |first=Preston |date=February 17, 2022 |title=What is Just Chatting on Twitch? |url=https://dotesports.com/streaming/news/what-is-just-chatting-on-twitch |access-date=March 14, 2022 |website=Dot Esports |language=en-US |archive-date=May 31, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220531112938/https://dotesports.com/streaming/news/what-is-just-chatting-on-twitch |url-status=live }}</ref> ''[[GeekWire]]'' reported that "while gameplay still makes up the vast majority of the content broadcast via Twitch, the 'Just Chatting' category—a catch-all term that encompasses anything from candid conversation to reality programming—took the top spot by a comfortable margin overall in December [2019]. While the category has been on the rise for the last couple of months, this was the first time that it's actually achieved No. 1 overall for a tracked period on the platform".<ref name="GeekWire-2020">{{cite web|date=January 9, 2020|title=Game streaming report: 'Just Chatting' category takes over Twitch; Facebook Gaming sees growth|url=https://www.geekwire.com/2020/game-streaming-report-just-chatting-category-takes-twitch-facebook-gaming-sees-growth/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225214618/https://www.geekwire.com/2020/game-streaming-report-just-chatting-category-takes-twitch-facebook-gaming-sees-growth/|archive-date=February 25, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=GeekWire|language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2020, ''[[Thrillist]]'' described Twitch as "talk radio for the [[extremely online]]".<ref>{{cite web|last=Corrall|first=Cody|date=November 18, 2020|title=The Museum of Home Video Is One of Twitch's Best-Kept, Weirdo Pop-Culture Secrets|url=https://www.thrillist.com/entertainment/nation/museum-of-home-video-twitch-channel|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201127053008/https://www.thrillist.com/entertainment/nation/museum-of-home-video-twitch-channel|archive-date=November 27, 2020|access-date=November 19, 2020|website=Thrillist}}</ref> Michael Espinosa, for ''[[Business Insider]]'' in 2021, highlighted that "Twitch dominates the live content space, with 17 billion hours watched last year (per StreamElements), compared to YouTube Gaming Live's 10 billion (per the company). But the vast majority of gaming content is still consumed on-demand, where YouTube is the clear leader with over 100 billion hours watched last year".<ref name="Espinosa-2021">{{cite web|last=Espinosa|first=Michael|date=October 6, 2021|title=Why Twitch is still the top destination for livestreaming, even as YouTube Gaming poaches some big streamers|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/twitch-youtube-battle-to-sign-top-streamers-nickmercs-drlupo-2021-10|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211008065558/https://www.businessinsider.com/twitch-youtube-battle-to-sign-top-streamers-nickmercs-drlupo-2021-10|archive-date=October 8, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=Business Insider|language=en-US}}</ref>

===As a teaching tool===
Twitch is often used for video game tutorials; the nature of Twitch allows mass numbers of learners to interact with each other and the instructor in real time.<ref name="Payne-2017">{{cite journal|last1=Payne|first1=Katherine|last2=Keith|first2=Mark J.|last3=Schuetzler|first3=Ryan M.|last4=Giboney|first4=Justin Scott|date=Dec 2017|title=Examining the learning effects of live streaming video game instruction over Twitch|journal=Computers in Human Behavior|volume=77|pages=95–109|doi=10.1016/j.chb.2017.08.029|doi-access=free}}</ref> Twitch is also used for software development learning,<ref name="Payne-2017"/> with communities of users streaming programming projects and talking through their work.

===Charity===
[[File:Summer Games Done Quick attendees (48149404692).jpg|thumb|right|[[Games Done Quick]] is a bi-annual [[speedrunning]] event for charity hosted on Twitch.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://associationsnow.com/2015/01/gaming-gurus-reinvented-telethons-web/ |publisher=Association Now |title=How Gaming Gurus Reinvented Telethons for the Web |author=Ernie Smith |date=January 13, 2015 |access-date=January 19, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160714025000/http://associationsnow.com/2015/01/gaming-gurus-reinvented-telethons-web/ |archive-date=July 14, 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]

Broadcasters on Twitch often host streams promoting and raising money towards charity. By 2013, the website has hosted events which, in total, raised over {{US$|8 million}} in donations for charitable causes, such as [[Extra Life (fundraiser)|Extra Life]] 2013.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://venturebeat.com/2013/10/31/livestreaming-community-on-twitch-has-raised-8-million-for-charity-plans-to-raise-more-this-weekend/ |title=Livestreaming community on Twitch has raised $8 million for charity; plans to raise more this weekend |website=VentureBeat |author=Jeffrey Grubb |date=October 31, 2013 |access-date=December 24, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131228135228/http://venturebeat.com/2013/10/31/livestreaming-community-on-twitch-has-raised-8-million-for-charity-plans-to-raise-more-this-weekend/ |archive-date=December 28, 2013 |url-status=live}}</ref> {{As of|2017|post=,}} Twitch has raised over US$75 million in donations for charitable causes.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://medium.com/twitch-news/2017-charity-update-twitch-community-gives-back-at-record-pace-a687f86001bd |title=2017 Charity Update: Twitch community gives back at record pace! |last=Schroeder |first=Andrew |date=July 20, 2017 |website=Twitch Blog ([[Medium (website)|Medium]]) |access-date=October 14, 2019 |archive-date=October 14, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191014111721/https://medium.com/twitch-news/2017-charity-update-twitch-community-gives-back-at-record-pace-a687f86001bd |url-status=live }}</ref> The biggest charity event of Twitch is [[ZEvent]], a French project created by [[ZeratoR|Adrien Nougaret]] and Alexandre Dachary, with more than US$10 million raised for [[Action Contre la Faim]] in October 2021.

===Esports===
{{See also|Twitch Rivals}}
[[File:1cun0472 Jpg (127168403).jpeg|thumb|right|The [[League of Legends World Championship|''League of Legends'' World Championship]] has been broadcast on Twitch annually since 2012.]]
[[ESL (company)|ESL]] tournaments have aired on Justin.tv and later Twitch.tv since 2009.<ref>{{cite web |title = ESL and DreamHack enter three-year broadcast deal with Twitch |url = https://www.esportsinsider.com/2020/04/esl-dreamhack-twitch-partnership/ |author = Jonno Nicholson |website = eSports Insider |date = April 28, 2020 |access-date = April 28, 2021 |archive-date = April 28, 2021 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210428003022/https://www.esportsinsider.com/2020/04/esl-dreamhack-twitch-partnership/ |url-status = live }}</ref> The platform has also been a longtime broadcaster of the [[Evolution Championship Series]].<ref>{{cite web |title=EVO tournament offering HD pay-per-view stream |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/2012-06-29-evo-tournament-offering-hd-pay-per-view-stream |author=Mike Williams |website=Games Industry |date=June 29, 2012 |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428013942/https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/2012-06-29-evo-tournament-offering-hd-pay-per-view-stream |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=EVO 2019: Schedule, Start Time and How to Stream Every Tournament Online |url=https://www.newsweek.com/evo-2019-schedule-start-time-how-stream-tournament-online-1452197 |author=Phillip Martínez |website=Newsweek |date=August 2, 2019 |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428013938/https://www.newsweek.com/evo-2019-schedule-start-time-how-stream-tournament-online-1452197 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Twitch has been the official broadcaster of the [[League of Legends World Championship|''League of Legends'' World Championship]] since 2012,<ref>{{cite web |title=The rise of Twitch.tv - How this giant came to be |url=https://www.mweb.co.za/games/view/tabid/4210/Article/13210/The-rise-of-Twitchtv-How-this-giant-came-to-be.aspx |author=Dreamer IX |website=MWeb Gamezone |date=May 15, 2014 |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428003117/https://www.mweb.co.za/games/view/tabid/4210/Article/13210/The-rise-of-Twitchtv-How-this-giant-came-to-be.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref> as well as other League of Legends tournaments organized by [[Riot Games]].

''[[Dota 2]]'''s premier tournament [[The International (Dota 2)|The International]] has been livestreamed on Twitch since 2013.<ref>{{cite web |title=The International attracts more than 1 million viewers |url=https://www.polygon.com/2013/8/14/4619742/the-international-attracts-more-than-1-million-viewers |author=Jenna Pitcher |website=Polygon |date=August 13, 2013 |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428013938/https://www.polygon.com/2013/8/14/4619742/the-international-attracts-more-than-1-million-viewers |url-status=live }}</ref>

The platform airs ''[[Rocket League]]'' tournaments organized by [[Psyonix]] since 2016.<ref>{{cite web |title=Twitch launching 'Rocket League' into eSports |url=https://fortune.com/2016/03/02/twitch-launching-rocket-league-into-esports/ |author=John Gaudiosi |website=Fortune |date=March 2, 2016 |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428003021/https://fortune.com/2016/03/02/twitch-launching-rocket-league-into-esports/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The ''[[ELeague]]'' also broadcasts events on Twitch since 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.timewarner.com/newsroom/press-releases/2015/09/24/turner-broadcasting-system-inc-and-wme-img-form-strategic|title=Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. and WME / IMG Form Strategic Partnership to Create Groundbreaking eSports League|website=[[Time Warner]]|date=September 24, 2015|access-date=November 20, 2015|archive-date=June 2, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170602182128/http://www.timewarner.com/newsroom/press-releases/2015/09/24/turner-broadcasting-system-inc-and-wme-img-form-strategic|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailydot.com/esports/turner-counter-strike-tbs/ |title=Turner plans to partner with an online streaming company, expand into other esports |first=Jared |last=Wynne |website=The Daily Dot |date=November 6, 2015 |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-date=November 10, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161110201317/http://www.dailydot.com/esports/turner-counter-strike-tbs/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Twitch and [[Blizzard Entertainment]] signed a two-year deal in June 2017 to make Twitch be the exclusive streaming broadcaster of select Blizzard esports championship events, with viewers under Twitch Prime earning special rewards in various Blizzard games.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://variety.com/2017/digital/news/twitch-blizzard-streaming-deal-overwatch-hearthstone-1202471111/ |title=Twitch and Blizzard Announce Two-Year Worldwide Collaboration |first=Jacob |last=Bryant |date=June 20, 2017 |access-date=June 20, 2017 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170620202810/http://variety.com/2017/digital/news/twitch-blizzard-streaming-deal-overwatch-hearthstone-1202471111/ |archive-date=June 20, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref> Twitch also reached a deal in 2018 to be the streaming partner of the [[Overwatch League]], with the site also offering an "All-Access Pass" with exclusive content, emotes, and in-game items for ''[[Overwatch (2016 video game)|Overwatch]]''.<ref>{{cite web === Professional sports ===

=== Emotes ===
Twitch features a large number of [[emote]]s. There are emotes free for all users, emotes for Turbo users, emotes for Twitch Prime users, and emotes for users who are subscribed to Twitch partners or affiliates.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://twitchemotes.com/ |title=Twitch Emotes – Bringing a little Kappa to you everyday |last=Community |first=The |website=twitchemotes.com |access-date=October 25, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171025185718/https://twitchemotes.com/ |archive-date=October 25, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref> {{As of|2024|May|post=,}} the most used emote is "x0pashL" with 8.85 billion uses, and the most used global emote is "TriHard" with 4.39 billion uses.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/why-a-former-twitch-employee-has-one-of-the-most-reproduced-faces-ever/ |title=How Kappa Became The Face Of Twitch |last=Goldenberg |first=David |date=October 21, 2015 |work=FiveThirtyEight |access-date=October 25, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171026001422/https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/why-a-former-twitch-employee-has-one-of-the-most-reproduced-faces-ever/ |archive-date=October 26, 2017 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://stats.streamelements.com/ |title=Chat stats |last=StreamElements |website=StreamElements |access-date=July 15, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180408010346/https://stats.streamelements.com/ |archive-date=April 8, 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref> Twitch partnered broadcasters unlock more "emote slots" as they gain more subscribers up to a maximum of 50 emotes per channel.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://help.twitch.tv/customer/portal/articles/2348985 |title=Subscriber Emoticon Tiers |website=Twitch Help |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107015354/https://help.twitch.tv/customer/portal/articles/2348985 |archive-date=November 7, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>

2018|title=Kappa dethroned on Twitch after six years on top|url=https://dotesports.com/culture/news/kappa-dethroned-on-twitch-after-six-years-on-top|url-status=live|access-date=January 7, shock.<ref name="Kelly-2021">{{cite web|last=Kelly|first=Makena|date=January 6, 2021|title=Twitch deletes PogChamp emote because it's now the face of 'further violence'|url=https://www.theverge.com/2021/1/6/22218088/twitch-bans-pogchamp-poggers-capitol-trump-violence-gootecks|website=The Verge|access-date=January 8, 2021|archive-date=January 8, (gamer)|Shroud]] (6.45 million followers) and [[TSM Myth]] (5.1 million followers).<ref>{{cite web|last=Webb|first=Kevin|date=October 2, 2019|title=The 10 most popular channels on [[TimTheTatman]], and [[Lirik (video game player)|Lirik]], who had a combined 10.36 million followers at the time.<ref name="Stephen-2019"/> [[Dr DisRespect]] signed a multi-year deal in March 2020.<ref name="Shanley-2020"/> In May 2020, Twitch signed popular streamers [[Summit1g]], [[dakotaz]] and JoshOG to multi-year exclusive deals.<ref>{{cite web|last=Woo|first=Ginny|title=Summit1G, web|last=Thier|first=Dave|title=Dr. Disrespect Banned From Twitch: Doc's Statement And What We
