{{As of|2022|8|post=,}} there have been eight streamers to have reached over 100,000 concurrent subscribers. These streamers are Ninja, Shroud, Ranboo, [[Ludwig Ahgren|Ludwig]], [[Casimiro (streamer)|Casimiro]], [[Ironmouse]], [[Gaules]] and [[Ibai Llanos|Ibai]].<ref>{{cite web|title=ALL-TIME SUBSCRIPTION RECORDS|url=https://twitchtracker.com/subscribers/all-time|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210323025554/https://twitchtracker.com/subscribers/all-time|archive-date=March 23, 2021|access-date=March 23, 2021|website=TwitchTracker}}</ref> In April 2021'', Business Insider'' reported that "over the past 31 days, Ahgren has streamed non-stop in an attempt to break the record of 269,154 subscribers held by gaming personality Tyler 'Ninja' Blevins. By the end of the month-long stream, Ahgren had over 282,000 subscribers on his channel. [...] At one point during his sleep cycle, his channel had the most concurrent viewers of any on the platform".<ref>{{cite web|last=Asarch|first=Steven|title=A Twitch streamer ended his 31-day livestream by breaking the record for the most-subscribed-to personality on the platform|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/ludwig-streaming-smash-stop-how-much-money-subathon-ended-twitch-2021-4|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210915075023/https://www.businessinsider.com/ludwig-streaming-smash-stop-how-much-money-subathon-ended-twitch-2021-4|archive-date=September 15, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=Business Insider|language=en-US}}</ref> In analysis of the October 2021 data leak, multiple [[news outlets]] reported that the three top-earning Twitch content creators are ''[[Critical Role]]'' ($9,626,712), [[xQc]] ($8,454,427), and Summit1g ($5,847,541).<ref name="BBC News-2021"/><ref name="Grayson-2021b"/><ref name="MarketWatch-2021">{{Cite news|date=October 6, 2021|title=Twitch hacker leaks entire source code and streamers' incomes for the past three years|work=[[MarketWatch]]|url=https://www.marketwatch.com/story/reported-twitch-hacker-leaks-entire-source-code-and-streamers-incomes-for-the-past-three-years-11633533597|url-status=live|access-date=October 6, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211006153725/https://www.marketwatch.com/story/reported-twitch-hacker-leaks-entire-source-code-and-streamers-incomes-for-the-past-three-years-11633533597|archive-date=October 6, 2021|quote=The leaked data does apparently reveal just how much money popular Twitch streamers are earning directly from Twitch. Some 81 have been paid more than $1 million by Twitch since August 2019, likely from subscriptions and advertising revenue, according to the leaked documents.}}</ref><ref name="Carpenter-2021">{{cite web|last=Carpenter|first=Nicole|date=October 6, 2021|title=Massive Twitch source code, creator earnings hack, explained|url=https://www.polygon.com/22713501/twitch-source-code-earnings-hack-explained|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211007134514/https://www.polygon.com/22713501/twitch-source-code-earnings-hack-explained|archive-date=October 7, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=Polygon|language=en-US}}</ref> Sisi Jiang, for ''[[Kotaku]]'', reported that "excluding streams that are run by multiple people (such as ''Critical Role''), there are no women in the top third of top-earning Twitch content creators"; in total, there are only three women in the top 100 and only one is a woman of color. Jiang highlighted that these streamers are "''Valorant'' streamer [[Pokimane]] at 39th place, cosplayer [[Amouranth]] at 48th, and music streamer Sintica at 71st" and commented that "in spite of the complaints about the 'hot tub meta,' 'titty streamers,' and how some male streamers perceive that female streamers are stealing views from men, the numbers show that only a small percentage of women are among the ranks of Twitch's highest-earning content creators".<ref>{{cite web|last=Jiang|first=Sisi|date=October 6, 2021|title=Only Three Percent Of Twitch's Top-Earning Streamers Are Women, Apparently|url=https://kotaku.com/only-three-percent-of-twitch-s-top-earning-streamers-ar-1847812847|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211007183646/https://kotaku.com/only-three-percent-of-twitch-s-top-earning-streamers-ar-1847812847|archive-date=October 7, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=Kotaku|language=en-us}}</ref>

In August 2021, DrLupo left Twitch for an exclusivity deal with YouTube;<ref>{{Cite news|last=Grayson|first=Nathan|date=August 30, 2021|title=Twitch star DrLupo signs exclusive YouTube deal, now 'secure for life'|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/2021/08/30/drlupo-twitch-youtube-exclusive-deal/|url-status=live|access-date=October 7, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210920175957/https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/2021/08/30/drlupo-twitch-youtube-exclusive-deal/|archive-date=September 20, 2021}}</ref> TimTheTatman followed in September 2021,<ref name="Grayson-2021a">{{Cite news|last=Grayson|first=Nathan|date=September 10, 2021|title=Why top streamers are leaving Twitch|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/2021/09/10/twitch-youtube-drlupo-timthetatman-leave-why/|access-date=October 7, 2021|issn=0190-8286|archive-date=July 2, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220702111355/https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/2021/09/10/twitch-youtube-drlupo-timthetatman-leave-why/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Espinosa-2021"/> as did Ludwig Ahgren in November 2021.<ref>{{cite web|last=Polhamus|first=Blaine|date=November 29, 2021|title=Ludwig moves to YouTube Gaming|url=https://dotesports.com/streaming/news/ludwig-moves-to-youtube-gaming|access-date=November 30, 2021|website=Dot Esports|language=en-US|archive-date=November 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211129234726/https://dotesports.com/streaming/news/ludwig-moves-to-youtube-gaming|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Moore|first=Jared|date=November 30, 2021|title=Record-Breaking Twitch Streamer Ludwig Moves Exclusively to YouTube Gaming|work=[[IGN]]|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/record-breaking-twitch-streamer-ludwig-moves-exclusively-to-youtube-gaming|access-date=November 30, 2021|archive-date=November 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130135005/https://www.ign.com/articles/record-breaking-twitch-streamer-ludwig-moves-exclusively-to-youtube-gaming|url-status=live}}</ref> Nathan Grayson, for ''[[The Washington Post]]'', commented that when streamers moved to Mixer in 2019, Twitch quickly locked down multiple streamers in exclusivity deals; however, streamers who moved to Mixer saw their audiences undergo "a marked downsizing. [...] It demonstrated that many viewers within Twitch's ecosystem, when deprived of their favorite big streamers, will just find other Twitch streamers to take their place. [...] Now Twitch is bargaining from a place of confidence. That allows it to reevaluate previous deals made when streamers had more leverage".<ref name="Grayson-2021a"/> Grayson reported that lower offers from Twitch coupled with Twitch's higher streaming hour requirement ("YouTube's contracts start at 100 hours of streaming time per month while Twitch's start at 200") has made YouTube's exclusivity deals "tantalizing" to some Twitch streamers. Grayson wrote that "[[Ryan Wyatt]], head of YouTube Gaming, said that allowing streamers to have a better work–life balance is a big priority for him"; DrLupo cited [[work–life balance]] as part of his decision to leave Twitch.<ref name="Grayson-2021a"/>

===Users===
It was reported in the early 2010s that the typical Twitch viewer is male and aged between 18 and 34 years of age, although the site has also made attempts at pursuing other demographics, including women.<ref name="Webb-2012"/> By 2015, Twitch had more than 100 million viewers per month.<ref name="Sarah Needleman-2015"/> In 2017, Twitch remained the leading live-streaming video service for video games in the US.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://techcrunch.com/2017/10/30/twitchs-concurrent-streamers-grew-67-in-q3-as-youtube-gaming-declined/ |title=Twitch's concurrent streamers grew 67% in Q3, as YouTube Gaming declined |first=Sarah |last=Perez |date=October 30, 2017 |access-date=November 8, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171108095718/https://techcrunch.com/2017/10/30/twitchs-concurrent-streamers-grew-67-in-q3-as-youtube-gaming-declined/ |archive-date=November 8, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://techcrunch.com/2017/04/18/streamers-flock-to-youtube-live-but-the-money-and-crowd-is-still-at-twitch/ |title=Streamers flock to YouTube Live, but the money (and crowd) is still at Twitch |first=Devin |last=Coldewey |date=April 18, 2017 |access-date=November 27, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201041200/https://techcrunch.com/2017/04/18/streamers-flock-to-youtube-live-but-the-money-and-crowd-is-still-at-twitch/ |archive-date=December 1, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref> ''GeekWire'' reported that "while Twitch's overall share of the streaming market has been steadily diminishing over the course of the year, from 67.1 percent in December 2018 to 61 percent at the end of the 2019, the steady growth of the overall market means that the overall amount of content watched on the service has done nothing but increase".<ref name="GeekWire-2020"/> The [[Academic journal|journal]] article ''World of Streaming. Motivation and Gratification on Twitch'' reported the results of a Twitch user survey in 2017.<ref name="Gros-2017">{{Cite book|last1=Gros|first1=Daniel|last2=Wanner|first2=Brigitta|last3=Hackenholt|first3=Anna|last4=Zawadzki|first4=Piotr|last5=Knautz|first5=Kathrin|title=Social Computing and Social Media. Human Behavior |chapter=World of Streaming. Motivation and Gratification on Twitch |date=2017|editor-last=Meiselwitz|editor-first=Gabriele|chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007%2F978-3-319-58559-8_5|url-status=live|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|language=en|location=Cham|publisher=Springer International Publishing|volume=10282|pages=44–57|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-58559-8_5|isbn=978-3-319-58559-8|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112001604/https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-58559-8_5|archive-date=November 12, 2020|access-date=October 7, 2021}}</ref> In ranking user motivations on the use of Twitch, users were motivated (in descending order) to watch Twitch: "to be entertained", "to follow gaming events", and to "have an alternative for television". Motivations classified as "socialization" and "information" ranked lower than motivations classified as "entertainment".<ref name="Gros-2017"/>

{{As of|2020|2|post=,}} it had 3 million broadcasters monthly and 15 million daily active users, with 1.4 million average [[concurrent user]]s.<ref name="DMR-2015"/><ref name="Perez-2018"/> [[Statista]], a company specializing in market and consumer data, reported that "as of May 2020, users in their teens and twenties accounted for more than three-quarters of Twitch's active app user accounts in the United States. According to recent data users aged 20 to 29 years, accounted for 40.6 percent of the video streaming app's user base on the [[Android (operating system)|Android]] platform".<ref>{{cite web|title=U.S. Twitch app users by age 2020|url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/1125170/twitch-app-us-users-age/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210408135153/https://www.statista.com/statistics/1125170/twitch-app-us-users-age/|archive-date=April 8, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=Statista|language=en}}</ref> They also reported that the "distribution of Twitch users in the United States as of 2nd quarter 2021" was 75% male and 25% female.<ref>{{cite web|title=Twitch users by gender in the U.S. 2021|url=https://www.statista.com/forecasts/1241866/twitch-us-user-share-by-gender|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211007193055/https://www.statista.com/forecasts/1241866/twitch-us-user-share-by-gender|archive-date=October 7, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=Statista|language=en}}</ref>

As of 2022, the countries with the most Twitch users were the [[United States]] (93 million), [[Brazil]] (16.9 million), [[Germany]] (16.8 million), [[France]] (15.4 million), the [[United Kingdom]] (13.4 million), [[Russia]] (10.5 million), [[Spain]] (10.5 million), [[Argentina]] (10 million), [[Mexico]] (9.2 million), and [[Italy]] (8.3 million users).<ref name="Twitch Users By Country 2023-2023">{{cite web |date=September 26, 2023 |title=Twitch Users By Country 2023 |url=https://worldpopulationreview.com/country-rankings/twitch-users-by-country |access-date=September 26, 2023 |archive-date=May 31, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240531043005/https://worldpopulationreview.com/country-rankings/twitch-users-by-country |url-status=live }}</ref> The United States accounts for roughly 36% of all Twitch users.<ref name="Twitch Users By Country 2023-2023" />

Twitch allows anyone to watch a live broadcast and does not require viewers to log in.<ref>{{cite web|date=November 10, 2020|title=Twitch: Everything You Need to Know|url=https://www.lifewire.com/what-is-twitch-4143337|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210809143315/https://www.lifewire.com/what-is-twitch-4143337|archive-date=August 9, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=Lifewire|language=en}}</ref> Users also have the option to follow and subscribe (also known as subbing) to streamers. Following is a free option, similar to other platforms such as Instagram and Twitter, where the user will see their followed streamers on the front page of Twitch when signed in and can receive notifications of specific broadcasts.<ref name="Lifewire-2020">{{cite web|last=|date=September 11, 2020|title=Twitch Subscriptions: What They Are and How They Work|url=https://www.lifewire.com/twitch-subscriptions-4147319|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412012845/https://www.lifewire.com/twitch-subscriptions-4147319|archive-date=April 12, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=Lifewire|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Morris">{{cite web|last=Morris|first=Tee|title=How to Follow and Subscribe to Twitch Channels|url=https://www.dummies.com/social-media/how-to-follow-and-subscribe-to-twitch-channels/|url-status=live|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=dummies|language=en|archive-date=October 7, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211007065944/https://www.dummies.com/social-media/how-to-follow-and-subscribe-to-twitch-channels/}}</ref> Subscribing is a way for users to financially support streamers in exchange for exclusive benefits determined by the individual streamer.<ref name="Lifewire-2020"/><ref name="Morris"/><ref>{{cite web|last=Delfino|first=Devon|date=May 14, 2020|title=How to subscribe to a channel on Twitch to show your support and unlock exclusive features|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/how-to-subscribe-on-twitch|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210817184138/https://www.businessinsider.com/how-to-subscribe-on-twitch|archive-date=August 17, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=Business Insider|language=en-US}}</ref> Users who link their Twitch account to their Amazon Prime account gain access to [[Prime Gaming]] which includes one complimentary Twitch subscription per month that the user can assign to the streamer of their choice.<ref name="Statt-2018"/><ref name="Peters-2020b"/><ref>{{cite web|last=Montelli|first=Chrissy|date=June 1, 2020|title='What is Twitch Prime?': The best features of Twitch's popular membership program, which comes bundled with Amazon Prime|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/what-is-twitch-prime|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210922192532/https://www.businessinsider.com/what-is-twitch-prime|archive-date=September 22, 2021|access-date=October 7, 2021|website=Business Insider|language=en-US}}</ref> The aforementioned 2017 academic survey stated that 31.5% of users "spent money on Twitch"; of those users, 22.6% "donated to a streamer", 31.6% subscribed to a streamer and 45.8% "did both". The majority of these users stated the "main motivation is to support a streamer financially".<ref name="Gros-2017"/> Twitch's Terms of Service does not allow people under 13 years of age to use its services. Additionally, people who are at least 13 years old but below the [[age of majority]] in their jurisdiction (18 in most jurisdictions), may only use the services under the supervision or permission of a parent or other legal guardian who agrees to abide to the Terms of Service.<ref>{{cite web|title=Terms of Service|url=https://www.twitch.tv/p/en/legal/terms-of-service/#2-use-of-twitch-by-minors-and-blocked-persons|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210430145924/https://www.twitch.tv/p/en/legal/terms-of-service/#2-use-of-twitch-by-minors-and-blocked-persons|archive-date=April 30, 2021|access-date=April 30, 2021|website=twitch.tv}}</ref>

===Partner and affiliate programs===
In July 2011, Twitch launched its Partner Program,<ref>{{cite news|last=Tassi|first=Paul|date=July 27, 2011|title=JustinTV Lets Gamers Earn Cash with New Twitch Partner Service|work=Forbes|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/insertcoin/2011/07/27/justintv-lets-gamers-earn-cash-with-new-twitch-partner-service/|url-status=live|access-date=September 17, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170825025320/https://forbes.com/sites/insertcoin/2011/07/27/justintv-lets-gamers-earn-cash-with-new-twitch-partner-service/|archive-date=August 25, 2017}}</ref> which reached over 11,000 members by August 2015.<ref>{{cite web|last=Grubb|first=Jeff|date=August 27, 2015|title=Twitch's partner contracts will keep most livestreamers from also using YouTube Gaming|url=https://venturebeat.com/2015/08/27/twitchs-partner-contracts-will-keep-most-livestreamers-from-also-using-youtube-gaming/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160422180127/http://venturebeat.com/2015/08/27/twitchs-partner-contracts-will-keep-most-livestreamers-from-also-using-youtube-gaming/|archive-date=April 22, 2016|access-date=May 18, 2016|website=VentureBeat}}</ref>

Similar to the Partner Program of other video sites like YouTube, the Partner Program allows popular content producers to share in the advertisement revenue generated from their streams. Additionally, Twitch users can subscribe to partnered streamers' channels for US$4.99 a month, often granting the user access to unique [[emoticons]], live chat privileges, and other various perks. Twitch retains US$2.49 of every US$4.99 channel subscription, with the remaining US$2.50 going directly to the partnered streamer.<ref>{{Cite news|title=How exactly do Twitch streamers make a living? Destiny breaks it down|work=Dot Esports|url=https://dotesports.com/culture/news/twitch-streaming-money-careers-destiny-1785#list-2|url-status=live|access-date=May 8, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180508185532/https://dotesports.com/culture/news/twitch-streaming-money-careers-destiny-1785#list-2|archive-date=May 8, 2018}}</ref> Although exceptions were made, Twitch previously required that prospective partners have an "average concurrent viewership of 500+", as well as a consistent streaming schedule of at least three days a week.<ref>{{cite web|author=Twitch|date=2014|title=Twitch Partner Signup|url=http://www.twitch.tv/partner/signup|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140404204205/http://www.twitch.tv/partner/signup|archive-date=April 4, 2014|website=Twitch}}</ref> However, since the launch of the 'Achievements' feature, there is a clearer "Path to Partnership" with trackable goals for concurrent viewership, duration and frequency of streams.<ref>{{cite web|author=Twitch|title=Customer Support|url=https://help.twitch.tv/s/article/achievements?language=en_US|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306235221/https://help.twitch.tv/s/article/achievements?language=en_US|archive-date=March 6, 2019|access-date=March 6, 2019|website=Twitch Help}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Engadget|author-link=Engadget|title=Twitch shows how close you are to becoming a paid streamer|url=https://www.engadget.com/2017/11/14/twitch-achievements/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306235332/https://www.engadget.com/2017/11/14/twitch-achievements/|archive-date=March 6, 2019|access-date=March 6, 2019|website=Engadget|date=November 14, 2017 }}</ref>

In April 2017, Twitch launched its "Affiliate Program" that allows smaller channels to generate revenue as well, also announcing that it would allow channels access to multi-priced subscription tiers.<ref>{{cite web|last=Fontaine|first=Robin|date=April 24, 2017|title=Twitch Affiliate Program launches today! First invites going out…|url=https://blog.twitch.tv/twitch-affiliate-program-launches-today-first-invites-going-out-9c020994a042|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190728141234/https://blog.twitch.tv/twitch-affiliate-program-launches-today-first-invites-going-out-9c020994a042|archive-date=July 28, 2019|access-date=March 6, 2019|website=Twitch Blog}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=April 19, 2017|title=Twitch's new subscription model will let fans pay streamers significantly more money|url=https://www.theverge.com/2017/4/19/15359244/twitch-new-subscription-model-tiers-more-money-streamers|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170420054028/http://www.theverge.com/2017/4/19/15359244/twitch-new-subscription-model-tiers-more-money-streamers|archive-date=April 20, 2017|access-date=April 20, 2017|website=The Verge|publisher=Vox Media}}</ref> The participants of this program get some but not all of the benefits of the Twitch Partners. Streamers can make profit from cheering with Bits which are purchasable from Twitch directly.<ref>{{cite web|date=April 24, 2017|title=Details on joining the Affiliate program|url=https://help.twitch.tv/customer/portal/articles/2785927-joining-the-affiliate-program|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170427003831/https://help.twitch.tv/customer/portal/articles/2785927-joining-the-affiliate-program|archive-date=April 27, 2017|access-date=April 26, 2017|work=Twitch}}</ref> Affiliates are also able to access the Twitch Subscriptions feature, with all the same functionality that Partners have access to, with a maximum of five subscriber emotes.{{citation needed|date=June 2024}} In September 2019, the service announced that Affiliates would now receive a share of ad revenue.<ref>{{cite web|author=<!-- None credited -->|date=September 27, 2019|title=TwitchCon Day 1: All the News from the Opening Ceremony|url=https://blog.twitch.tv/en/2019/09/27/twitchcon-day-1-all-the-news-from-the-opening-ceremony/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210206184252/https://blog.twitch.tv/en/2019/09/27/twitchcon-day-1-all-the-news-from-the-opening-ceremony/|archive-date=February 6, 2021|access-date=October 31, 2019|work=Twitch Blog}}</ref>

Additionally, in June 2023, Twitch introduced the Partner Plus Program. This program was designed to recognize Twitch partners who consistently bring a large audience and engagement to the platform. Streamers in this program receive a 70/30 revenue share on subscription revenue. To qualify for the program, creators had to maintain a sub count of at least 350 subscribers for three consecutive months.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Introducing the Partner Plus Program |url=https://blog.twitch.tv/en/2023/06/15/introducing-the-partner-plus-program/ |access-date=2024-11-05 |website=blog.twitch.tv |language=en}}</ref> Once that is complete, qualifying members will be enrolled for the next 12 months. The program was officially launched on October 1, 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Spangler |first=Todd |date=2023-06-15 |title=Twitch Will Pay Out 70% of Subscription Revenue to Qualifying Streamers Under New 'Partner Plus' Program |url=https://variety.com/2023/digital/news/twitch-partner-plus-70-percent-revenue-split-streamers-1235645488/ |access-date=2024-11-05 |website=Variety |language=en-US}}</ref> This enabled partners to earn more as they continue to grow their community. However, a number of streamers were not happy with the program. Streamers argued that it excluded certain creators because of the criteria and that creators would burn themselves out by trying to achieve 350 monthly subscribers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sung |first=Morgan |date=2023-06-20 |title=Twitch's new Partner Plus tier strains an already tense relationship with creators |url=https://techcrunch.com/2023/06/20/twitch-revenue-split-partner-plus-angers-creators/ |access-date=2024-11-05 |website=TechCrunch |language=en-US}}</ref>

In January 2024, Twitch made some changes to the program. The platform announced that it would be introducing a new tier to its revenue share program that would grant a 60/40 revenue split and has lower requirements.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sung |first=Morgan |date=2024-01-24 |title=Twitch announces 60/40 revenue split in expanded Plus Program |url=https://techcrunch.com/2024/01/24/twitch-announces-60-40-revenue-split-in-expanded-plus-program/ |access-date=2024-11-05 |website=TechCrunch |language=en-US}}</ref> In addition, the program would also become open to affiliates, expanding access to smaller creators. The program is now known as the "Plus Program." When the program was first launched the year prior, Twitch would only pay out the 70/30 revenue split until streamers made $100,000. Along with expanding the Partner Plus Program and adding a new revenue level, Twitch also announced that it would be eliminating the $100,000 cap for the 70/30 revenue share for all streamers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=An Update to Several Streamer Payout Programs |url=https://blog.twitch.tv/en/2024/01/24/an-update-to-several-streamer-payout-programs/ |access-date=2024-11-05 |website=blog.twitch.tv |language=en}}</ref> This was part of Twitch's strategy to provide more earning opportunities for streamers. The program uses a points system to determine which revenue split a streamer qualifies for. Each monthly subscription counts towards the points total. However, some subscriptions have higher point values. One tier 1 subscription is one point, one tier 2 subscription is two points, and one tier 3 subscription equals six points.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nightingale |first=Ed |date=2024-01-24 |title=Twitch expands programme for improved revenue share to more streamers |url=https://www.eurogamer.net/twitch-expands-programme-for-improved-revenue-share-to-more-streamers |access-date=2024-11-05 |website=Eurogamer.net |language=en}}</ref> To qualify for the 60/40 revenue split, streamers must maintain 100 Plus Points for three consecutive months. For the 70/30 revenue split, streamers must maintain 300 Plus Points.

Advertising on the site has been handled by a number of partners. In 2011, Twitch had an exclusive deal with [[Future US]].{{citation needed|date=June 2024}} On April 17, 2012, Twitch announced a deal to give [[CBS Interactive]] the rights to exclusively sell advertising, promotions and sponsorships for the community.<ref>{{cite web|date=April 17, 2012|title=CBS Interactive Expands Into Esports Category With Exclusive Live Gaming Video and League Partnerships|url=http://www.majorleaguegaming.com/news/major-league-gaming-partners-with-cbs-interactive|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120419124307/http://www.majorleaguegaming.com/news/major-league-gaming-partners-with-cbs-interactive|archive-date=April 19, 2012|access-date=April 17, 2012|website=Major League Gaming}}</ref> On June 5, 2013, Twitch announced the formation of the Twitch Media Group, a new in-house advertisement sales team which has taken over CBS Interactive's role of selling advertisements.<ref name="Lawler-2013"/>

For users who do not have ad-free access to a channel or Twitch Turbo, pre-roll advertising, and mid-roll commercial breaks that are manually triggered by the streamer, are displayed on streams. In September 2020, Twitch announced that it would test automated mid-roll advertising on streams, which cannot be controlled by the streamer.<ref>{{cite web|last=Stephen|first=Bijan|date=September 15, 2020|title=Twitch is testing mid-roll ads that streamers can't control|url=https://www.theverge.com/2020/9/15/21437787/twitch-midroll-ad-affiliate-partner-cpm|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200917045742/https://www.theverge.com/2020/9/15/21437787/twitch-midroll-ad-affiliate-partner-cpm|archive-date=September 17, 2020|access-date=September 17, 2020|website=The Verge|language=en}}</ref>

==Content moderation and restrictions==
===Copyrighted content===
On August 6, 2014, Twitch announced that all on-demand videos on Twitch became subject to [[acoustic fingerprint]]ing using software provided by content protection company [[Audible Magic]]; if copyrighted music (particularly, songs played by users from outside of the game they are playing) is detected, the 30-minute portion of the video which contains the music will be muted. Live broadcasts were not subject to these filters.<ref>{{cite web |title=Twitch Mimics YouTube, Begins Automatically Muting Videos With Copyrighted Audio |url=http://www.gamespot.com/articles/twitch-mimics-youtube-begins-automatically-muting-/1100-6421554/ |website=GameSpot |publisher=CBS Interactive |access-date=August 7, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140810025643/http://www.gamespot.com/articles/twitch-mimics-youtube-begins-automatically-muting-/1100-6421554/ |archive-date=August 10, 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Twitch Will Mute Copyrighted Music in On-Demand Videos |url=https://recode.net/2014/08/06/twitch-will-mute-copyrighted-music-in-on-demand-videos/ |access-date=August 8, 2014 |work=Re/code |date=August 6, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808020515/http://recode.net/2014/08/06/twitch-will-mute-copyrighted-music-in-on-demand-videos/ |archive-date=August 8, 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref> A system was available for those who believed they were inappropriately affected and had rights to the music they used to challenge the filtering.<ref>{{cite web |title=Twitch CEO apologizes for how new policies rolled out, says improvements are coming |url=https://www.engadget.com/2014/08/07/twitch-changes/ |website=Engadget |date=August 8, 2014 |access-date=August 8, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808061416/http://www.engadget.com/2014/08/07/twitch-changes/ |archive-date=August 8, 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref> Twitch offered a selection of [[Production music#Royalty-free libraries|royalty-free music]] for streamers to use, which was expanded upon later in January 2015.<ref name="PC World-2015">{{cite web |title=Twitch adds a music section, free tracks to make up for copyright crackdown |url=http://www.pcworld.com/article/2871255/twitch-adds-a-music-section-free-tracks-to-make-up-for-copyright-crackdown.html |website=PC World |date=January 15, 2015 |access-date=January 15, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150116072957/http://www.pcworld.com/article/2871255/twitch-adds-a-music-section-free-tracks-to-make-up-for-copyright-crackdown.html |archive-date=January 16, 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref> The audio filtering system, along with the lack of communication surrounding the changes in general, proved to be controversial among users. In a [[Reddit]] AMA, co-founder Emmett Shear admitted that his staff had "screwed up" and should have provided advance warning of the changes, and promised that Twitch had "absolutely no intention" of implementing audio filtering on live broadcasts.<ref>{{cite news |title=Under Fire, Twitch CEO Says "We Screwed Up" Policy Announcement |url=http://recode.net/2014/08/07/under-fire-twitch-ceo-says-we-screwed-up-policy-announcement/ |access-date=August 8, 2014 |work=Re/code |date=August 7, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140810004334/http://recode.net/2014/08/07/under-fire-twitch-ceo-says-we-screwed-up-policy-announcement/ |archive-date=August 10, 2014 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In June 2020, Twitch received a large wave of [[DMCA]] takedown notices aimed at year-old VODs and "clips" (short segments of streams that can be captured by users) that contain copyrighted music from 2017 to 2019. Twitch complied with the takedowns and also issued a number of copyright strikes against viewers. Concerned streamers were notified that they should remove all VODs and clips if not certain they did not contain copyrighted material. This provoked major backlash, both at the loss of prior content but also based on viability concerns due to an inability to review or even rapidly delete content. There were also complaints based that strikes were being issued on viewer-created clips, even where the streamer-created content was deleted.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/twitch-users-face-potential-channel-bans-following-platforms-sudden-influx-of-dmca-music-takedown-requests/|title=TWITCH USERS FACE POTENTIAL CHANNEL BANS FOLLOWING PLATFORM'S 'SUDDEN INFLUX OF DMCA MUSIC TAKEDOWN REQUESTS'|publisher=Music Business Worldwide|author=Murray Stassen|date=June 8, 2020|access-date=June 9, 2020|archive-date=June 9, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200609142327/https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/twitch-users-face-potential-channel-bans-following-platforms-sudden-influx-of-dmca-music-takedown-requests/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotaku.com/after-massive-dmca-takedown-twitch-streamers-are-delet-1843954430|title=After Massive DMCA Takedown, Twitch Streamers Are Deleting Thousands Of Clips|publisher=Kotaku|author=Nathan Grayson|date=June 8, 2020|access-date=June 9, 2020|archive-date=June 9, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200609142707/https://kotaku.com/after-massive-dmca-takedown-twitch-streamers-are-delet-1843954430|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pcgamer.com/twitch-has-been-hit-by-a-wave-of-copyright-claims-over-old-clips/|title=Twitch has been hit by a wave of copyright claims over old clips|publisher=PC Gamer|author=Fraser Brown|date=June 8, 2020|access-date=June 9, 2020|archive-date=June 9, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200609142336/https://www.pcgamer.com/twitch-has-been-hit-by-a-wave-of-copyright-claims-over-old-clips/|url-status=live}}</ref>

On September 15, 2020, Twitch signed a licensing agreement with the French performance society [[SACEM]], allowing composers and publishers to collect royalties whenever their music is streamed in France. Twitch already had licensing deals with the American societies [[ASCAP]], [[Broadcast Music, Inc.|BMI]], [[SESAC]] and [[Global Music Rights]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://completemusicupdate.com/article/sacem-announces-licensing-deal-with-twitch/|title=SACEM announces licensing deal with Twitch &#124; Complete Music Update|access-date=April 28, 2021|archive-date=April 28, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428084921/https://completemusicupdate.com/article/sacem-announces-licensing-deal-with-twitch/|url-status=live}}</ref>

To address these issues and also build upon the growth of music-based content on Twitch, Twitch introduced an extension known as "Soundtrack" in September 2020, which plays rights-cleared music with curated genre-based playlists. It is contained within a separate audio track that is not recorded with VODs,<ref>{{Cite magazine|last=Blistein|first=Jon|date=October 1, 2020|title=Twitch Licenses Music Now. But the Music Industry Says It's Skirting the Rules|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/pro/features/twitch-soundtrack-licensing-sync-1069411/|access-date=November 11, 2020|magazine=Rolling Stone|language=en-US|archive-date=November 13, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201113205855/https://www.rollingstone.com/pro/features/twitch-soundtrack-licensing-sync-1069411/|url-status=live}}</ref> and had agreements with 24 music distributors and independent record labels at launch.<ref>{{cite web|date=September 30, 2020|title=Twitch, still unlicensed by majors, launches rights-cleared music via deals with indie distributors and labels|url=https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/twitch-still-unlicensed-by-majors-launches-rights-cleared-music-via-deals-with-indie-distributors-and-labels/|access-date=October 1, 2020|website=Music Business Worldwide|language=en-US|archive-date=October 3, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201003123924/https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/twitch-still-unlicensed-by-majors-launches-rights-cleared-music-via-deals-with-indie-distributors-and-labels/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Twitch launches a rights-cleared music catalog for streamers, Soundtrack by Twitch|url=https://techcrunch.com/2020/09/30/twitch-launches-a-rights-cleared-music-catalog-for-streamers-soundtrack-by-twitch/|access-date=October 1, 2020|website=TechCrunch|date=September 30, 2020|language=en-US|archive-date=January 24, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230124181615/https://techcrunch.com/2020/09/30/twitch-launches-a-rights-cleared-music-catalog-for-streamers-soundtrack-by-twitch/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Stephen|first=Bijan|date=September 30, 2020|title=Twitch's Soundtrack feature debuts today, and it will let streamers play music while they're live|url=https://www.theverge.com/2020/9/30/21495243/twitch-soundtrack-streaming-music-soundcloud-distrokid-facebook-gaming|access-date=October 1, 2020|website=The Verge|language=en|archive-date=September 30, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200930162415/https://www.theverge.com/2020/9/30/21495243/twitch-soundtrack-streaming-music-soundcloud-distrokid-facebook-gaming|url-status=live}}</ref> A group of US [[Performance rights organisation|performance rights]] and music associations accused Twitch of designing Soundtrack in such a way as to avoid payment of [[Mechanical license|mechanical]] and [[synchronization license]]s—claims which Twitch has defended.<ref>{{cite web|last=Stephen|first=Bijan|date=November 12, 2020|title=In Twitch's fight with the music industry, streamers are paying the price|url=https://www.theverge.com/2020/11/12/21562372/twitch-soundtrack-riaa-music-youtube|access-date=December 15, 2020|website=The Verge|language=en|archive-date=December 22, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222054045/https://www.theverge.com/2020/11/12/21562372/twitch-soundtrack-riaa-music-youtube|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Aswad|first=Jem|date=October 26, 2020|title=Twitch, Amazon Slammed by RIAA and Major Industry Groups for Using Unlicensed Music; Twitch Disputes Claim|url=https://variety.com/2020/digital/news/twitch-amazon-unlicensed-music-riaa-recording-academy-1234815503/|access-date=December 15, 2020|website=Variety|language=en-US|archive-date=October 9, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211009040304/https://variety.com/2020/digital/news/twitch-amazon-unlicensed-music-riaa-recording-academy-1234815503/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In September 2021, Twitch and the [[National Music Publishers' Association]] signed a creative partnership.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/twitch-strikes-deal-with-music-publishers |title=Twitch Strikes Deal with Music Publishers |website=MusicBusinessWorldwide.com |date=September 21, 2021 |access-date=September 27, 2021 |url-status=live |archive-date=October 9, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211009040248/https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/twitch-strikes-deal-with-music-publishers }}</ref>

In September 2024, Twitch introduced a new program for [[Disk jockey|DJs]] on the platform, allowing them access to a new stream category for [[DJ mix]]es where music from participating labels may be streamed without the risk of a DMCA takedown, with a share of revenue being used to pay royalties (for affiliates and partners, this is deducted from the channel's existing split). This program has limitations: features such as VODs and clips are disabled on any channel enrolled in the DJ program, even if streaming non-DJ content (with Twitch officially recommending the use of a separate account for non-DJ streams), and DJs are restricted to playing music from certain labels and publishers that have reached agreements with the service (potentially restricting the ability to play unofficial remixes).<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Trew |first=James |title=Twitch's New DJ Program Has Flaws, But It's the Best There Is |url=https://www.wired.com/story/twitchs-new-dj-program-may-be-doomed-but-its-the-best-there-is/ |access-date=2024-09-25 |magazine=Wired |language=en-US |issn=1059-1028}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Sato |first=Mia |date=2024-06-06 |title=Twitch announces a program allowing DJs to split revenue with record labels |url=https://www.theverge.com/2024/6/6/24172320/twitch-dj-revenue-share-record-labels-music-licensing |access-date=2024-09-25 |website=The Verge |language=en}}</ref>

===Mature content===
Twitch users are not allowed to stream any game that is rated "Adults Only" (AO) in the United States by the [[Entertainment Software Rating Board]] (ESRB), regardless of its rating in any other geographical region, and any game that contains "overtly sexual content" or "gratuitous violence", or content which violates the terms of use of third-party services.<ref>{{cite web |title=Twitch pulls the plug on CS:GO gambling broadcasts |url=http://www.polygon.com/2016/7/14/12187460/twitch-csgo-gambling |website=Polygon |date=July 14, 2016 |publisher=Vox Media |access-date=July 16, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160715153639/http://www.polygon.com/2016/7/14/12187460/twitch-csgo-gambling |archive-date=July 15, 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Polygon-2015"/>

Twitch has also explicitly banned specific games from streaming, regardless of rating; this includes games such as ''[[BMX XXX]]'', [[eroge]] [[visual novel]] games (such as ''[[Dramatical Murder]]''), ''[[HuniePop]]'', ''[[Rinse and Repeat]]'', ''[[Second Life]]'', and ''[[Yandere Simulator]]''.<ref name="Polygon-2015">{{cite web |title=Twitch bans Adults Only-rated games from streaming |url=http://www.polygon.com/2015/5/27/8675141/twitch-bans-adults-only-rated-games-from-streaming-esrb |website=Polygon |date=May 27, 2015 |publisher=Vox Media |access-date=May 28, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528053619/http://www.polygon.com/2015/5/27/8675141/twitch-bans-adults-only-rated-games-from-streaming-esrb |archive-date=May 28, 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=List of prohibited games |url=https://help.twitch.tv/customer/portal/articles/1992676-list-of-prohibited-games |website=Twitch Help Center |access-date=January 12, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170113142322/https://help.twitch.tv/customer/portal/articles/1992676-list-of-prohibited-games |archive-date=January 13, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Polygon-2016">{{cite web |title=Yandere Simulator banned from Twitch streaming |url=http://www.polygon.com/2016/1/22/10815594/yandere-simulator-banned-twitch-reddit |website=Polygon |date=January 22, 2016 |publisher=Vox Media |access-date=January 28, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129023548/http://www.polygon.com/2016/1/22/10815594/yandere-simulator-banned-twitch-reddit |archive-date=January 29, 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Shower simulator Rinse and Repeat makes the Twitch shortlist for banned games |url=http://www.polygon.com/2015/9/24/9394327/shower-simulator-rinse-and-repeat-makes-the-twitch-shortlist-for |access-date=January 28, 2016 |work=Polygon |publisher=Vox Media |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160211232454/http://www.polygon.com/2015/9/24/9394327/shower-simulator-rinse-and-repeat-makes-the-twitch-shortlist-for |archive-date=February 11, 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref> The banning of ''Yandere Simulator'' was criticized by [[YandereDev]], the developer of the game. He believed that the game was being arbitrarily singled out with no explanation, as Twitch has not banned other games with sexual or violent content such as ''[[Mortal Kombat X]]'', ''[[Grand Theft Auto]]'', or ''[[The Witcher 3]]''.<ref name="Polygon-2016"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Yandere Simulator Dev Says Twitch Hasn't Told Him Why His Game Was Banned |url=http://kotaku.com/yandere-simulator-dev-says-twitch-hasnt-told-him-why-hi-1754533741 |website=Kotaku |date=January 22, 2016 |access-date=January 28, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160126070013/http://kotaku.com/yandere-simulator-dev-says-twitch-hasnt-told-him-why-hi-1754533741 |archive-date=January 26, 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Twitch took temporary action in May 2019 after channels related to the video game ''[[Artifact (video game)|Artifact]]'' began to be used for inappropriate content. ''Artifact'', a major game by [[Valve Corporation|Valve]], had lost most of its audience in just months from its release, and by late May 2019, several popular [[livestream]]ers commented that the total viewership for ''Artifact'' streams had dropped to near zero. In the days that followed, several streamers started to make streams purporting to be ''Artifact'' gameplay but was [[trolling]] or other off-topic content. Initially these new streams were playing with the viewers or were jokes, such as showing animal videos or ''[[League of Legends]]'' matches. After a few days, other ''Artifact'' channel streams appeared containing content that was against the terms of Twitch's use policy, including full copyrighted movies, pornography, Nazi propaganda, and at least one stream that showed the entirety of the shooter's video from the [[Christchurch mosque shootings]]. The titles of such streams were usually presented to imply they were showing other content while waiting in queue for ''Artifact'' matches as to appear legitimate. As word of these streams in the ''Artifact'' section grew, Twitch took action, deleting the account that streamed the Christchurch shooting.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.polygon.com/2019/5/27/18641498/artifact-twitch-section-trolling |title=Twitch's Artifact section has become a waking nightmare |first=Cass |last=Marshall |date=May 27, 2019 |access-date=May 28, 2019 |work=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190527231805/https://www.polygon.com/2019/5/27/18641498/artifact-twitch-section-trolling |archive-date=May 27, 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref> Twitch then took steps to temporarily ban new accounts from streaming until it can resolve the issue.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theverge.com/2019/5/28/18643167/twitch-artifact-suspend-new-users-trolls-attack-valve |title=Twitch is temporarily suspending new creators from streaming after troll attack |first=Julia |last=Alexander |date=May 28, 2019 |access-date=May 28, 2019 |work=[[The Verge]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190528213635/https://www.theverge.com/2019/5/28/18643167/twitch-artifact-suspend-new-users-trolls-attack-valve |archive-date=May 28, 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref> By June 2019, Twitch started taking legal actions against one hundred "John Doe" streamers in a California court, accusing them of trademark infringement, breach of contract, fraud, and unlawful use of the service that was harming and scaring away users of the service.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-06-15/twitch-sues-troll-streamers-over-violent-videos-pornography |title=Twitch Sues Troll Streamers Over Violent Videos, Pornography |first=Robert |last=Burnson |date=June 15, 2019 |access-date=June 15, 2019 |work=[[Bloomberg L.P.]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190616111551/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-06-15/twitch-sues-troll-streamers-over-violent-videos-pornography |archive-date=June 16, 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.usgamer.net/articles/twitch-lawsuit-blames-artifact-porn-streams-for-permanently-pushing-users-off-the-platform |title=Twitch Lawsuit Blames Artifact Porn Streams for Permanently Pushing Users Off the Platform |first=Matt |last=Kim |date=June 19, 2019 |access-date=June 19, 2019 |work=[[USGamer]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190619225833/https://www.usgamer.net/articles/twitch-lawsuit-blames-artifact-porn-streams-for-permanently-pushing-users-off-the-platform |archive-date=June 19, 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In early 2021, some streams began to use their Twitch channel to broadcast themselves from [[hot tub]]s while wearing swimsuits. Twitch considered these streams to be "not advertiser friendly", banning some of the more predominant channels that had taken this route. In May 2021, Twitch clarified in a "Pools, Hot Tubs, and Beaches" post that it was not trying to discriminate against women or others through this action, but through content that it deemed to be "sexually suggestive".<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamer.com/twitch-addresses-hot-tub-streaming-controversy-by-adding-a-hot-tub-category/ | title = Twitch addresses hot tub streaming controversy by adding a hot tub category | first = Andy | last = Chalk | date = May 21, 2021 | access-date = June 21, 2021 | work = [[PC Gamer]] | archive-date = June 24, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210624203213/https://www.pcgamer.com/twitch-addresses-hot-tub-streaming-controversy-by-adding-a-hot-tub-category/ | url-status = live }}</ref> In June that year, Twitch also took similar action against users that performed [[yoga]] while at the same time made [[autonomous sensory meridian response]] (ASMR) sounds via their microphones, which Twitch also stated was approaching sexual content.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/22543478/twitch-amouranth-indiefoxx-yoga-asmr-stream-hot-tub-meta-ban | title = Twitch bans popular streamers Amouranth and Indiefoxx after yoga ASMR streams | first = Ana | last = Diaz | date = June 21, 2021 | access-date = June 21, 2021 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] | archive-date = June 21, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210621171903/https://www.polygon.com/22543478/twitch-amouranth-indiefoxx-yoga-asmr-stream-hot-tub-meta-ban | url-status = live }}</ref>

In December 2023, the platform introduced a new policy that relaxed prohibitions on certain adult content, given that said content would be appropriately labeled. This came amidst the popularity of supposedly "topless" videos on the platform. Popularized by streamer [[Morgpie]], the genre saw creators push the previous boundaries of Twitch's guidelines by implying but not explicitly showing nudity.<ref>{{cite web|last=Sung|first=Morgan|url=https://techcrunch.com/2024/01/03/twitch-shuts-down-topless-meta-with-attire-policy-update/|title=Twitch attire policy update shuts down the viral topless meta|work=[[TechCrunch]]|date=January 3, 2024|access-date=March 15, 2025}}</ref> Twitch's new policy also allowed depictions of "fictionalized nudity". However, Twitch rescinded its policy very shortly after, following backlash from users and streamers.<ref>{{cite web|last=Bailey|first=Kat|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/twitch-new-sexual-content-guidelines-artistic-nudity|title=Twitch's New Sexual Content Guidelines Updated to Include 'Artistic Nudity' After Viral Topless Stream|work=[[IGN]]|date=December 15, 2023|access-date=March 15, 2025}}</ref> Twitch CEO Dan Clancy acknowledged that the new policy was a step too far, and that distinguishing between digital art and photography was challenging. As a result, Twitch will no longer permit depictions of real or fictional nudity, regardless of the medium. The company also removed content that violated the updated policy and issued channel enforcements. While some changes to Twitch's Sexual Content Policy remain in effect, such as allowing content that highlights certain body parts and specific dances without a label, games featuring nudity or sexual violence as a core focus are still prohibited.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://variety.com/2023/digital/news/twitch-reverses-artistic-nudity-sexual-content-policy-1235841288/ | title = Twitch Reverses Policy Allowing 'Artistic Nudity,' Citing AI's Ability to Create Realistic Images | first = Todd | last = Spangler | date = December 15, 2023 | access-date = December 17, 2023}}</ref>

===Hate speech and harassment===
In February 2018, Twitch updated its acceptable content policies to direct that any content that it deemed hateful be suspended from its platform.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.engadget.com/2018-02-08-twitch-updates-hate-speech-harassment-sexual-content-policies.html | title = Twitch updates policies on hate speech, harassment and sexual content | first = Rob | last = LeFebvre | date = February 8, 2018 | access-date = June 30, 2020 | work = [[Engadget]] | archive-date = July 29, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200729092421/https://www.engadget.com/2018-02-08-twitch-updates-hate-speech-harassment-sexual-content-policies.html | url-status = live }}</ref>

In June 2020, a number of women stepped forward with accusations towards several streamers on Twitch and other services related to sexual misconduct and harassment claims.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/video-game-streaming-platforms-investigating-allegations-sexual-harassment-n1231689 | title = Video game streaming platforms investigating allegations of sexual harassment | first = Kalhan | last = Rosenblatt | date = June 23, 2020 | access-date = June 23, 2020 | work = [[NBC News]] | archive-date = June 23, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200623210333/https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/video-game-streaming-platforms-investigating-allegations-sexual-harassment-n1231689 | url-status = live }}</ref> Twitch stated it would review all reported incidents and comply with law enforcement in any investigative efforts. However, several popular streamers on Twitch's service believed that the platform could do more to evaluate the accused individuals, prevent incidents, and protect others in the future, and used June 24, 2020, as a Twitch blackout day, not streaming any content through Twitch to show their support.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/twitch-blackout-calls-grow-game-industry-culture-change-1300093 | title = Amid Twitch Blackout, Calls Grow for Game Industry Culture Change | first = Trilby | last = Beresford | date = June 24, 2020 | access-date = June 24, 2020 | work = [[The Hollywood Reporter]] | archive-date = June 25, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200625083202/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/twitch-blackout-calls-grow-game-industry-culture-change-1300093 | url-status = live }}</ref> By the evening of June 24, 2020, Twitch had placed several bans on the accounts of those accused after completing its investigation, and stated in a blog post it would be forwarding additional details to law enforcement.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.engadget.com/twitch-abuse-bans-051617639.html | title = Twitch responds to sexual abuse accusations, bans several streamers | first = Richard | last = Lawler | date = June 24, 2020 | access-date = June 24, 2020 | work = [[Engadget]] | archive-date = June 25, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200625072554/https://www.engadget.com/twitch-abuse-bans-051617639.html | url-status = dead }}</ref>

Twitch temporarily suspended an account belonging to then [[President of the United States|US President]] [[Donald Trump]]'s campaign on June 29, 2020. Twitch stated that "hateful conduct is not allowed" as the reason for the suspension.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.cnn.com/2020/06/29/tech/twitch-suspends-trump-account/index.html | title = Twitch suspends Trump campaign account | first = Brian | last = Fung | date = June 29, 2020 | access-date = June 30, 2020 | work = [[CNN]] | archive-date = June 29, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200629224231/https://www.cnn.com/2020/06/29/tech/twitch-suspends-trump-account/index.html | url-status = live }}</ref>

Twitch announced a new policy towards harassment and hateful content in December 2020 that would take effect on January 22, 2021, aimed to better protect marginalized users of the service. While the new policy is more strict, Twitch said that this also includes a larger sliding scale of remedies or punishments to better deal with edge cases, such as temporarily blocking one's channel for a short time rather than a full ban. The new rules include a ban on imagery containing the [[Flags of the Confederate States of America|Confederate Flag]], and 'racist emotes', though the list of such emotes has not been clarified yet.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.theverge.com/2020/12/9/22165342/twitch-hateful-conduct-harassment-policy-update | title = Twitch overhauls its rules around harassment and hateful conduct | first = Bijan | last = Stephen | date = December 9, 2020 | access-date = December 9, 2020 | work = [[The Verge]] | archive-date = February 17, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210217185817/https://www.theverge.com/2020/12/9/22165342/twitch-hateful-conduct-harassment-policy-update | url-status = live }}</ref> The new policy included banning words that were considered sexual insults, such as "[[incel]]" and "[[virgin]]" when used for harassment. The banned words included "[[simp]]", which raised criticism by streamers and long-time viewers. While its slang origins have defined "simp" derogatorily as "a man who invests a lot of time and energy into women who don't want him", the term had become common on Twitch as an insult related to men being nice to women on the service or simply to refer to a person with loyalty to another. Twitch, in response, clarified that penalties for using these terms would only be enforced if they were being used in harassment of other users.<ref>{{cite web|last=Kastrenakes|first=Jacob|date=December 16, 2020|title=Twitch bans "simp"|url=https://www.theverge.com/2020/12/16/22179256/twitch-bans-simp-virgin-incel-new-sexual-harassment-policy|access-date=December 16, 2020|website=The Verge|language=en|archive-date=March 27, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210327103625/https://www.theverge.com/2020/12/16/22179256/twitch-bans-simp-virgin-incel-new-sexual-harassment-policy|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.dailydot.com/debug/twitch-simp-ban-insult/ | title = Twitch won't let you call people 'simp' anymore | first = Bryan | last = Rolli | date = December 17, 2020 | access-date = December 17, 2020 | work = [[The Daily Dot]] | archive-date = May 14, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210514040242/https://www.dailydot.com/debug/twitch-simp-ban-insult/ | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamer.com/twitch-outlaws-simp-and-incel-as-sexually-disparaging-insults/ | title = Twitch outlaws 'simp' and 'incel' as sexually disparaging insults | first = Andy | last = Chalk | date = December 17, 2020 | access-date = December 17, 2020 | work = [[PC Gamer]] | archive-date = December 17, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201217011211/https://www.pcgamer.com/twitch-outlaws-simp-and-incel-as-sexually-disparaging-insults/ | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://kotaku.com/twitch-is-cracking-down-on-simp-emotes-because-of-haras-1843347454 | title = Streamers Flabbergasted After Twitch Partially Bans The Word 'Simp' | first = Nathan | last = Grayson | date = December 17, 2020 | access-date = December 17, 2020 | work = [[Kotaku]] | archive-date = May 14, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210514040204/https://kotaku.com/twitch-is-cracking-down-on-simp-emotes-because-of-haras-1843347454 | url-status = live }}</ref>

On December 4, 2020, Twitch removed the "blind playthrough" tag due to concerns of [[ableism]] that it may be offensive to those who are [[visually impaired]]. Suggestions for non-offensive and more neutral labels include "first playthrough", "undiscovered," and "no spoilers."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotaku.com/twitch-removes-blind-playthrough-tag-after-disability-c-1845813019|title=Twitch Removes 'Blind Playthrough' Tag After Disability Criticism|date=December 4, 2020|access-date=April 30, 2021|archive-date=March 2, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210302060139/https://kotaku.com/twitch-removes-blind-playthrough-tag-after-disability-c-1845813019|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{anchor|Raid}}
A popular feature of Twitch is the ability to "raid" another channel, where multiple users, coordinated from a different Twitch channel or another social media service, all join a target channel to provide support and encouragement. This is typically used to help boost the popularity of the target channel, particularly if the raid is organized by a popular streamer. Twitch had officially supported this type of activity since 2017 with the ability for a streamer to send all of their viewers to another channel as a raid.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://venturebeat.com/2017/10/20/twitch-officially-incorporates-channel-raids-and-other-new-features/ | title = Twitch reveals official channel raids and new ways to make money | first = Jeff | last = Grubb | date = October 20, 2017 | access-date = August 24, 2021 | work = [[Venture Beat]] | archive-date = January 25, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210125210216/https://venturebeat.com/2017/10/20/twitch-officially-incorporates-channel-raids-and-other-new-features/ | url-status = dead }}</ref> However, around mid-2021, new types of "hate raids" began to occur with increasing frequency on Twitch. In these cases, numerous users would flood a channel and its chat with messages of harassment and hate towards the streamer as a form of [[cyberbullying]]. Most of these users are typically from [[automated bot]]s, which made it difficult for channel moderators to deal with the amount of messages.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.theverge.com/22633874/how-to-stop-a-hate-raid-twitch-safety-tools | title = How to stop a hate raid | first = Ash | last = Parrish | date = August 20, 2021 | access-date = August 22, 2021 | work = [[The Verge]] | archive-date = August 22, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210822000606/https://www.theverge.com/22633874/how-to-stop-a-hate-raid-twitch-safety-tools | url-status = live }}</ref> Despite warning Twitch about these hate raids, Twitch had shown little action towards stopping them, leading numerous streams to organize a "#ADayOffTwitch" on September 1, 2021, as a form of protest in anticipation that Twitch will find ways to take action against them.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2021-08-22-twitch-streamers-organise-adayofftwitch-in-protest-of-hate-raids | title = Twitch streamers organise #ADayOffTwitch in protest of hate raids | first = Vikki | last = Blake | date = August 22, 2021 | access-date = August 22, 2021 | work = [[Eurogamer]] | archive-date = August 22, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210822155721/https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2021-08-22-twitch-streamers-organise-adayofftwitch-in-protest-of-hate-raids | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2021-09-02-twitch-streamers-adayofftwitch-protest-hits-platform-viewer-totals | title = Twitch streamers' big #ADayOffTwitch protest hits platform viewer totals | first = Tom | last = Phillips | date = September 2, 2021 | access-date = September 2, 2021 | work = [[Eurogamer]] | archive-date = September 2, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210902120711/https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2021-09-02-twitch-streamers-adayofftwitch-protest-hits-platform-viewer-totals | url-status = live }}</ref> After acknowledging a problem with dealing with hate raids, Twitch launched a lawsuit in early September 2021 against two individuals it had determined to be responsible for managing several hate raids after permanently banning their accounts.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.gamespot.com/articles/twitch-sues-two-alleged-hate-raiders/1100-6496124/?ftag=CAD-01-10abi2f | title = Twitch Sues Two Alleged Hate Raiders | first = Jenny | last = Zheng | date = September 10, 2021 | access-date = September 10, 2021 | work = [[GameSpot]] | archive-date = September 10, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210910174717/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/twitch-sues-two-alleged-hate-raiders/1100-6496124/?ftag=CAD-01-10abi2f | url-status = live }}</ref> At the end of September 2021, Twitch introduced tools for streamers to be able to limit who may participate in their chat as to prevent hate raids. These tools allow streamers to limit chat to those that have verified their phone number or email with Twitch, as well as to those that have followed their channel for a minimum amount of time.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/22700564/twitch-hate-raids-safety-feature-streaming | title = Twitch announces new features to curb hate raids | first = Ana | last = Diaz | date = September 29, 2021 | access-date = September 29, 2021 | work = [[The Verge]] | archive-date = September 29, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210929181815/https://www.polygon.com/22700564/twitch-hate-raids-safety-feature-streaming | url-status = live }}</ref>

In May 2022, following the [[2022 Buffalo shooting|mass shooting in Buffalo]], the New York state attorney general's office announced an investigation into multiple online platforms, including Twitch, to determine their part in platforming or promoting hateful content. The investigation will also focus on the platforms' moderation efforts. A spokesperson for Twitch stated that the service would comply with the investigation.<ref>{{cite web |last=Roth |first=Emma |title=NY attorney general is investigating Twitch, Discord, and 4chan over Buffalo shooting |url=https://www.theverge.com/2022/5/18/23125783/ny-attorney-general-launches-investigation-twitch-discord-buffalo-shooting |website=The Verge |date=May 18, 2022 |access-date=May 22, 2022 |archive-date=May 20, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220520154456/https://www.theverge.com/2022/5/18/23125783/ny-attorney-general-launches-investigation-twitch-discord-buffalo-shooting |url-status=live }}</ref>

In November 2024, Twitch banned the use of [[Zionist as a pejorative|"Zionist" as a slur]]. Twitch specified that the rule was conditional, saying, "You're allowed to discuss the political movement of that name, but not attack or demean another individual or group of people on the basis of their background or religious belief."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parrish |first=Ash |date=2024-11-15 |title=Twitch says 'Zionist' can be a punishable slur. |url=https://www.theverge.com/2024/11/15/24297474/twitch-says-zionist-can-be-a-punishable-slur |access-date=2024-11-16 |website=The Verge |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Andy Chalk-2024">{{Cite news |author1=Andy Chalk |date=2024-11-15 |title=Twitch forbids the use of 'Zionist' to 'attack or demean,' but says you can still use it to talk about the political movement |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/software/platforms/twitch-forbids-the-use-of-zionist-to-attack-or-demean-but-says-you-can-still-use-it-to-talk-about-the-political-movement/ |access-date=2024-11-16 |work=PC Gamer |language=en}}</ref> The [[Anti-Defamation League]], [[non-governmental organization]] that was founded to combat [[antisemitism]], took credit for the change.<ref>{{Cite news |author1=Rich Stanton |date=2024-10-22 |title=Under pressure from pro-Israel group, Twitch bans several Arab streamers over a month-old TwitchCon panel |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/gaming-industry/under-pressure-from-pro-israel-group-twitch-bans-several-arab-streamers-over-a-month-old-twitchcon-panel/ |access-date=2025-12-31 |work=PC Gamer === Extremism ===

In April 2021, it was reported that Twitch was providing a financial lifeline to extremists such as [[QAnon]] adherents and far-right influencers.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Browning |first=Kellen |date=2021-04-27 |title=Extremists Find a Financial Lifeline on Twitch |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/04/27/technology/twitch-livestream-extremists.html |access-date=2022-10-11 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=October 11, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221011043540/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/04/27/technology/twitch-livestream-extremists.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Another report in August and September 2021, by the Institute of Strategic Dialogue also identified Twitch as a platform where far right extremists run rampant. Clips from far-right extremists, such as 'Omegle Redpilling' become quite popular before they are removed from the platform and in some cases, are not removed at all according to [[Institute for Strategic Dialogue|ISD]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gaming and Extremism: The Extreme Right on Twitch |url=https://www.isdglobal.org/isd-publications/gaming-and-extremism-the-extreme-right-on-twitch/ |access-date=2022-10-11 |website=ISD |language=en-GB |archive-date=October 11, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221011043541/https://www.isdglobal.org/isd-publications/gaming-and-extremism-the-extreme-right-on-twitch/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |title=How the far right took over Steam and Discord |language=en-GB |magazine=Wired UK |url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/steam-discord-far-right |access-date=2022-10-11 |issn=1357-0978 |archive-date=October 11, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221011043543/https://www.wired.co.uk/article/steam-discord-far-right |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2024, it was reported that new Twitch account sign‑ups from Israeli IP addresses had been blocked for an extended period. In public posts that month, Twitch claimed it had temporarily disabled email‑verified sign‑ups in [[Israel]] after the [[October 7 attacks|October 7, 2023]] attacks to prevent graphic content, and further stated the block was inadvertently left in place, calling this an "unacceptable miss." Twitch also asserted phone verification remained available, a point disputed by many users. The restriction was lifted in October 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-21 |title=Following year-long ban, Twitch publicly enables sign-ups from Israeli IP addresses |url=https://www.jpost.com/diaspora/article-825477 |access-date=2024-10-21 |website=[[The Jerusalem Post]] |language=en |issn=0792-822X}}</ref>

=== Gambling ===
On September 20, 2022, Twitch announced that beginning October 18, it would prohibit the streaming of slots, roulette and dice games on [[online gambling|gambling websites]] not licensed in the US or "other jurisdictions that provide sufficient consumer protection". The policy change does not affect [[sports betting]], [[fantasy sport]]s, and [[poker]].<ref name="BBC News-2022">{{Cite news |date=2022-09-21 |title=Twitch announces slots and roulette gambling ban |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-62982509 |access-date=2022-09-27 |archive-date=September 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220927141158/https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-62982509 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Washington Post">{{Cite news |title=Twitch cracks down on gambling, but streamers aren't sure it's enough |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/2022/09/21/twitch-gambling-ban-pokimane-mizkif-xqc/ |access-date=2022-09-27 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Community Guidelines |url=https://safety.twitch.tv/s/article/Community-Guidelines |publisher=Twitch Interactive, Inc. |access-date=24 April 2023}}</ref> Gambling has been extremely popular on Twitch for years, being one of the most popular types of content on the platform, with many streamers being sponsored by online gambling services; however, it has also been controversial, with prominent streamers such as [[Mizkif]] and Pokimane speaking out against the negative effects of gambling streams.<ref name="BBC News-2022"/><ref name="Washington Post"/> The announcement came shortly after a popular streamer admitted he spent $200,000 in donations on ''CS:GO'' [[skin gambling]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-19 |title=Top Twitch Streamers Like Pokimane, Mizkif Threaten Strike After $200,000 Gambling Scam |url=https://kotaku.com/twitch-gambling-scam-pokimane-mizkif-hasanabi-strike-1849554448 |access-date=2022-09-27 |website=Kotaku |language=en-us |archive-date=September 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220927141157/https://kotaku.com/twitch-gambling-scam-pokimane-mizkif-hasanabi-strike-1849554448 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Internet censorship==
{{As of|2018|9|20|post=,|df=US}} the Twitch website is blocked and the app is blocked from the [[App Store (Apple)|Apple App Store]] in [[China]].<ref>[https://www.theverge.com/2018/9/20/17883736/twitch-china-block-app-store Twitch is now blocked in China] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181002060548/https://www.theverge.com/2018/9/20/17883736/twitch-china-block-app-store|date=October 2, 2018}} – Shannon Liao, [[The Verge]], September 20, 2018</ref>

In [[India]], Twitch was reportedly blocked by [[Reliance Industries|Reliance]]-owned telecommunication company [[Jio]] as well as internet service providers [[JioFiber]] and [[Hathway]] in September 2020 as some users were illegally streaming [[Indian Premier League]] [[cricket]] matches on the platform.<ref>{{cite news|title=Jio Blocking Twitch Streams During IPL 2020 Cricket Matches, Users Report|language=en|work=NDTV|url=https://gadgets.ndtv.com/telecom/news/jio-twitch-block-streams-ipl-2020-cricket-matches-reliance-hathway-users-report-2301985|access-date=November 17, 2020|archive-date=November 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201119204120/https://gadgets.ndtv.com/telecom/news/jio-twitch-block-streams-ipl-2020-cricket-matches-reliance-hathway-users-report-2301985|url-status=live}}</ref> Later it was unblocked.{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}}

[[Slovakia]]'s government reportedly blocked Twitch in June 2021 after a streamer in the country with around 35,000 followers was found streaming poker, which was in violation of local gambling laws.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jr |first=Anthony James Puleo |date=2021-06-24 |title=Twitch Banned in An Entire Country Because of One Streamer |url=https://gamerant.com/twitch-banned-slovakia-one-streamer/ |access-date=2023-01-23 |website=[[Game Rant]] |language=en |archive-date=January 23, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230123092417/https://gamerant.com/twitch-banned-slovakia-one-streamer/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Nikolova |first=Milana |date=2021-07-19 |title=Slovakia bans popular live streaming platform over e-gambling concerns |url=https://emerging-europe.com/news/slovakia-bans-popular-live-streaming-platform-over-e-gambling-concerns/ |access-date=2023-01-23 |website=Emerging Europe |language=en-GB |archive-date=January 23, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230123092418/https://emerging-europe.com/news/slovakia-bans-popular-live-streaming-platform-over-e-gambling-concerns/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

On July 4, 2022, the [[Iran]]ian government blocked access to Twitch for Iranian Internet users.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ir.voanews.com/a/new-wave-filtering-twitch-discord-iran/6644220.html |title=موج جدید فیلترینگ با مسدود شدن "توییچ" و کندی "دیسکورد" در ایران |language=fa |publisher=Voice of America |date=July 4, 2022 |access-date=July 10, 2022 |archive-date=July 9, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220709213330/https://ir.voanews.com/a/new-wave-filtering-twitch-discord-iran/6644220.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

On February 23, 2024, Twitch was blocked in [[Turkey]] per a complaint by the country's lotteries commission.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-02-24 |title=Turkey bans access to streaming services Twitch and Kick |url=https://www.duvarenglish.com/turkey-bans-access-to-streaming-services-twitch-and-kick-news-63899 |access-date=2024-02-25 |website=Duvar English |language=tr-TR}}</ref> Service was restored in the country six days later on February 29.{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}}

=== Twitch Desktop App and CurseForge ===
After acquiring [[Curse LLC]], Twitch Interactive rebranded the Curse app as the Twitch Desktop App in March 2017. It kept features for [[Video game modding|mod]] installation and management for supported games via [[CurseForge]]; kept Curse Voice features such as screen sharing, text chat, voice chat, video chat and community server creation; added a dedicated browser for the Twitch website; added Twitch's friends system; and added activity sharing. This update also redesigned the application.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://techcrunch.com/2017/03/10/twitch-to-relaunch-curse-acquired-last-year-as-the-more-social-twitch-desktop-app/ |title=Twitch to }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-03-10 |title=Twitch rebrands Curse desktop app to compete with Discord and Steam |url=https://venturebeat.com/business/twitch-rebrands-curse-desktop-app-to-compete-with-discord-and-steam/ |access-date=2023-05-04 |website=VentureBeat |language=en-US}}</ref> The software also served as the client for the former Twitch Game Store.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://blog.twitch.tv/the-new-twitch-desktop-app-is-here-6d6a71c6ec83 |title=The new Twitch Desktop App is here |last=Petrocelli === Creator Dashboard ===
The Creator Dashboard on Twitch is a tool that helps streamers manage and optimize their channels. In 2019, the platform announced a new set of features to make streaming more accessible and interactive. This new Creator Dashboard introduced features such as Stream Manager, Quick Actions, Creator Updates, and Assistant.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Takahashi |first=Dean |date=2019-12-04 |title=Twitch introduces new dashboard so more people can create livestreams |url=https://venturebeat.com/business/twitch-introduces-new-dashboard-so-more-people-can-create-livestream-programming/ |access-date=2024-11-05 |website=VentureBeat |language=en-US}}</ref> These features were introduced so that creators could set subscriber goals, analyze engagement trends, and simplify streaming tasks. The Stream Manager allows streamers to view various aspects of their livestream such as their live chat, recent followers and subscribers, and a playback of the stream to see what the viewers are seeing.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Irén |first=David |url=https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/record.jsf?pid=diva2:1679358&dswid=9299 |title=Designing a second screen application to assist streamers increase live stream interactivity |date=2022}}</ref> The Quick Actions panel on the Creator Dashboard allows streamers to perform actions such as running ads, enabling followers-only or emote-only chat, and creating clips. The Creator Updates section is a dedicated space for streamers to learn about important product updates and feature changes. The Assistant section provides creators with resources to help them grow their channel and become an affiliate or partner.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Everything to know about the new Creator Dashboard |url=https://blog.twitch.tv/en/2019/12/04/everything-to-know-about-the-new-creator-dashboard/ |access-date=2024-11-05 |website=blog.twitch.tv |language=en}}</ref>
